FLASHCARD SET · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Kitchen Things flashcards.

Thirty-five cards that name the busiest room in the house, sorted into age pills so parents know exactly what is on the menu: the everyday things a three-year-old already uses, the helper tools a four- or five-year-old can start with, the grown-up tools older kids love to name and one card — the chef’s knife — that exists to teach the kitchen’s biggest rule: knives are for grown-ups. The class game is Kitchen Helper: find the item, say its name, then sort the cards into "I can use it" and "grown-ups only."

THE CARDS

Every card in the set.

Each card has its own page, and every card shows its age pill — start with the group that fits your child today.

Ages 3 and up

The everyday kitchen kids see every day and can already use: spoon, fork, plate, mug, bowl, kettle, fridge, microwave, toaster, trash bin — plus the pans and the dishwasher.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    Play Kitchen Helper

    The class game in three steps: the child finds the item, says its name, then sorts the card into one of two piles — "I can use it" and "grown-ups only." The sorting IS the safety lesson, and every child’s piles are a little different, which makes a great family conversation.

  2. 02

    Follow the age pills

    Every card carries an age pill. Start with the Ages 3+ cards, graduate to the helper tools at four or five, and let the Ages 6+ cards stay a name-only game until small hands are ready. Nothing needs to be rushed — the pills do the pacing.

  3. 03

    Run the hot-check

    Spread the cards face up and ask: which ones get HOT? The kettle, the saucepan, the frying pan, the baking tray, the microwave, the toaster. Every hot card gets a toy oven mitt dropped on it — a sorting game that teaches the kitchen’s most important rule while it plays.

  4. 04

    Cook one real thing

    Pick the simplest helper card — measuring cups in banana muffins, a whisk in pancake batter, a rolling pin on cookie dough — and cook it together. The card names the tool, the kitchen uses the tool, and the recipe does the rest.

      Baking Tray Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Hot — don’t touch

      The gray metal tray — the baking tray carries the cookies into the oven, and it comes out the same shape but a completely different temperature: hot, hot, hot.

      Say it together

      “Baking tray! The cookie tray. Dough balls go on the tray… spaced apart… into the oven it slides. And when it comes out — HOT! The tray is a hot one — grown-ups lift it, mitts go on, we never touch.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Your child’s job is the arranging: dough balls spaced on the tray (they spread — "give each cookie room for its neighbour"), then the tray goes to the oven by the grown-up. When the DING comes, watch the oven-mitt parade — tray out, onto the rack — and repeat the rule: "the tray is hot; we wait." Waiting is the job; cookies are the prize.

      Quick parent note

      The baking tray is the clearest hot-things teacher because kids SEE it change state: same tray, safe to fill and hold before, untouchable after. Spacing dough also sneaks in spacing math. The wait-after-the-DING habit is oven safety installed at cookie speed.

      Teach it, step by step

      Blender Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 6+Sharp — careful

      The white machine with the tall jug — the blender whirs fruit into smoothies in twenty seconds, and it hides the sharpest blades in the kitchen at the bottom of that jug. Loud, fast, grown-up.

      Say it together

      “Blender! The whirring machine. Fruit and milk go in the jug… lid on TIGHT… press the button — WHIRRR! Everything spins into a smoothie. The blades inside are SHARP — grown-ups handle the jug. We listen, we watch, we drink the smoothie!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name it and run the ritual from a safe step away: fruit in (by you both), lid on tight (the grown-up’s click), button pressed by the grown-up — and your child is the smoothie announcer: "WHIRRR! It’s spinning!" Pour, drink, declare it the best smoothie yet. The blades stay a fact, not a fear: sharp things, grown-up hands, lid always on.

      Quick parent note

      The blender’s blade lesson matters because its danger is invisible — hidden under the jug, spinning too fast to see. "Lid on, blades are grown-ups’" said cheerfully at every smoothie builds the rule where it counts. And a child who helped make the smoothie has never once refused to drink it.

      Teach it, step by step

      Box Grater Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 6+Sharp — careful

      The tall four-sided tower with the holes — the box grater shreds cheese and carrots into little strips, and every hole on it is sharp, which makes it a look-and-learn tool for now.

      Say it together

      “Box grater! The four-sided tower. The cheese rubs up and down the big holes… SHRED — little cheese ribbons! Careful: the holes are SHARP. Look with your eyes, not your fingers.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      This is a name-and-watch card: find the grater, count its four sides, notice the different hole sizes (big shreds, small shreds, slices). Then watch a grown-up grate cheese — palm flat on top, fingers far away — and say the sharp-things rule together: "sharp things are grown-up things." The cheese on pasta afterwards tastes like a science demo.

      Quick parent note

      The grater card earns its place in the sharp-things lesson: it looks friendly and behaves sharp. Learning "the holes are blades" at six, by looking, is exactly the safe introduction — graters cause more little-finger scrapes than knives, and this card is the antidote.

      Chef’s Knife Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Grown-ups onlyKnives are for grown-ups

      The kitchen’s sharpest tool — the chef’s knife does the serious chopping on the serious board, and this card exists for one reason: to teach the kitchen’s biggest rule out loud, early, and kindly.

      Say it together

      “Chef’s knife! The big, sharp knife. This is the kitchen’s most important rule: KNIVES ARE FOR GROWN-UPS. Not today, not with help — grown-ups only. Your jobs are the butter knife, the spoon, the whisk. The chef’s knife waits for big hands, years from now.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Say the rule at the drawer, at the counter, at every chopping session — the same words, until the child says them first: "knives are for grown-ups." Give the sharp respect without the fear: the knife is a great tool that stays in the grown-up zone. Then point at the child’s own tools — the butter knife, the board, the banana to slice — so helping never stops, it just uses the right tools.

      Quick parent note

      Owner’s rule, taught straight: "knives are for grown-ups." The knife stays on the card and on the wall because hiding sharp things makes them fascinating, while naming them makes them understood. A child who knows the rule, the reason and their own safe tools is the safest child in the kitchen — and in a few years, on a board like this one, they will start again with a butter knife exactly the way they started here.

      Teach it, step by step

      Coffee Maker Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 6+Hot — don’t touch

      The machine with the glass jug — the coffee maker drips hot water through coffee grounds into the pot, and its plate keeps the jug warm all morning. Hot machine, hot jug: a look-and-learn member of the hot family.

      Say it together

      “Coffee maker! The morning machine. Water goes in the top, coffee in the filter… drip, drip, drip — the jug fills up! The jug and the plate stay HOT. We never touch the coffee maker — grown-ups pour.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name it on the counter and watch a brew from the outside: water in, filter in, button on — drip drip drip. Say the rule while it drips: "the jug is hot; grown-ups only." Then the best part — your child can pour the COLD drinks instead: juice for the table, water for the cups. Everyone has a pouring job; the coffee maker’s job just belongs to the grown-ups.

      Quick parent note

      The coffee maker is the kitchen’s most familiar "hands-off" machine, which makes it a low-drama place to rehearse the hot rule: it hums, it drips, it steams, and the child’s job is simply to let it work. Meanwhile the cold-drink pouring job keeps small hands in the serving business, safely.

      Colander Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The green bowl full of holes — the colander lets water escape and keeps the food in, which is exactly the magic kids want to know about: where does the pasta water GO?

      Say it together

      “Colander! The bowl with holes. In go the grapes… water on… woooosh — the water runs through the holes and the grapes stay in! The colander drains the water away.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Wash fruit together: grapes or berries in the colander, your child works the tap, watches the water through the holes and shakes the bowl gently to dry. Then the grand demo — draining pasta (grown-up carries the hot pot, your child holds the colander steady in the sink). Holes that hold food and lose water: kitchen physics, visible.

      Quick parent note

      The colander teaches the filter idea — let liquid through, keep the solid — which shows up again in sieves, strainers and tea bags for the rest of life. Washing fruit in it is also a zero-risk job with a genuine result: clean fruit the washer is proud to eat.

      Teach it, step by step

      Cooking Spoon Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Safe to use

      The wooden spoon that stirs everything — the cooking spoon is the first tool of every little helper, big enough to grip, blunt enough to trust, and always up for a stir.

      Say it together

      “Cooking spoon! The big wooden spoon. Hold it like this… stir, stir, stir the batter. Round and round — you are the stirrer today!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Fill a bowl with dry oats, hand over the spoon and let your child stir to their heart’s content — stirring dry is zero mess and all practice. Then promote the spoon to a real job: pancake batter, cake mix, scrambled eggs. The stir is the toddler’s signature on the meal.

      Quick parent note

      Stirring is grip strength, wrist control and patience in one motion. The wooden spoon is the classic first tool because it cannot cut, cannot scratch and forgives every enthusiastic swirl — which is exactly what a three-year-old’s stirring looks like.

      Teach it, step by step

      Cutting Board Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The flat wooden board — the cutting board is where chopping happens, and it has a job kids love: it holds the food still and keeps the counter safe while little chefs work.

      Say it together

      “Cutting board! The wooden board for chopping. The food goes ON the board — never chop without the board! Your banana goes here, your butter knife does the cutting… safe and steady.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Set up the board with a banana and a butter knife (the kid-safe kind): slice the banana into coins for cereal or a snack. The board stays still, the butter knife cuts soft food, the fingers stay clear. Then upgrade to soft strawberries or cheese cubes. Chopping is the proudest kitchen job there is — the board is what makes it safe.

      Quick parent note

      The board card teaches a rule and a skill together: chopping happens on the board (never in the hand, never on the counter), and soft foods get the butter knife. Real slicing jobs with safe tools are how young cooks earn their way toward bigger knives — years later, on boards just like this one.

      Teach it, step by step

      Dishwasher Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Safe to use

      The white machine under the counter — the dishwasher washes the dishes so nobody has to, and it offers children the perfect first kitchen job: loading the basket with the safe, unbreakable things.

      Say it together

      “Dishwasher! The machine that washes the dishes. In go the plates… the cups… the spoons. Click, the door shuts — whoosh, wash wash wash! Then everything comes out clean and warm.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Give your child the cutlery basket: spoons in spoon-side-up (or down — pick your family’s rule and keep it), one at a time, into their spots. Sorting silverware is matching practice that ends with a machine full of clean dishes. Unloading the cups to the low shelf is the promotion, saved for when the loading is expert.

      Quick parent note

      The dishwasher is the gentlest appliance in the kitchen — no flame, no blade, no heat the child can reach — which makes it the natural first chore machine. A child who loads a dishwasher learns sorting, care and the big idea that everyone’s plate gets washed together.

      Food Thermometer Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 6+Grown-up tools

      The thin probe with the digital screen — the food thermometer checks that the inside of the food is properly cooked, which is how kitchens know the food is safe, not just looking safe.

      Say it together

      “Food thermometer! The temperature checker. The pointy end goes IN the food… the screen shows a number — how hot the inside is! When the number is high enough, the food is properly cooked. Science you can eat!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name it and watch it work: a grown-up checks a roast or a pot of soup, your child reads the number on the screen. Ask: "is the number big enough? Is the food ready?" It is a fine what-is-this demo — and it plants the big idea early: cooks check the inside, not just the outside. Numbers that keep people safe.

      Quick parent note

      The thermometer card is kitchen science and kitchen safety in one: temperature is invisible, but a number makes it visible. For the Ages 6+ crew the lesson is the checking habit itself — the best cooks measure. Someday your child will own one; today they know its name and its job.

      Teach it, step by step

      Fork Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Safe to use

      The spiky tool with the green handle — the fork is the workhorse of every meal, and using it well is one of the quiet milestones of eating independently.

      Say it together

      “Fork! The pointy fork has four little teeth. Hold it in your fist… push it into the food… lift… and EAT! You did it with a fork!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Practise on the easiest wins first: banana coins, soft-cooked potato, melon cubes. Show the push-and-lift, then let the wobbly spearing happen — every skewered piece is a victory lap. Knife-and-fork teamwork comes later; today the fork does the whole show.

      Quick parent note

      Fork control is real fine-motor work: aim, push, lift, steady. It also moves a child from finger food to table food — a small step with a large side effect of pride. A child-size fork with a fat handle shortens the learning curve by months.

      Teach it, step by step

      Frying Pan Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Hot — don’t touch

      The black pan with the green handle — the frying pan makes the sizzle sound every kid knows: eggs, pancakes, bacon. And like everything on the stove, it is firmly in the hot, don’t-touch family.

      Say it together

      “Frying pan! Sizzle sizzle — the pan is cooking! The pan gets VERY hot, and the oil jumps. We never touch the frying pan — grown-ups only. You crack the eggs at the counter, and the pan does the sizzling.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Split the job: your child cracks and whisks the eggs at the counter (the real, proud-making work), while the grown-up works the hot pan. When the sizzle starts, run the safety call — "sizzling means step back!" — and let your child declare it. The sizzle becomes the sound of a rule working.

      Quick parent note

      The frying pan’s spitting oil makes it the most jump-worthy hot thing in the kitchen, so the rule is said early and often. Meanwhile the crack-an-egg job keeps little hands fully in the cooking — separation of hot and helpful is the whole trick of cooking with kids.

      Teach it, step by step

      Funnel Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 6+Grown-up tools

      The little gray cone with the stem — the funnel guides a pour into a small opening without a drop lost: water, oil, juice, all delivered neatly into bottles that would otherwise splash everywhere.

      Say it together

      “Funnel! The little cone helper. Stand it in the bottle mouth… pour — the liquid runs down the funnel, right into the bottle! No spills, no puddles. The funnel makes every pour neat.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name it and try it with supervision: funnel in an empty bottle, and your child pours water from a jug — watch it glide through, zero mess. Then the reverse question: what happens with NO funnel? (A puddle. A glorious puddle, outside, where puddles are allowed.) Cause and effect, demonstrated pour-ably.

      Quick parent note

      The funnel is engineering in one word: change a wide pour into a narrow stream. It belongs on the Ages 6+ shelf because the concept — guiding flow — is the point more than the tool. Kids who can explain WHY the funnel works have discovered fluid dynamics at the kitchen sink.

      Teach it, step by step

      Garlic Press Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 6+Grown-up tools

      The green squeezer with the little basket — the garlic press crushes a clove of garlic into tiny pieces in one squeeze, and it is one of those kitchen tools kids see and immediately ask: what IS that?

      Say it together

      “Garlic press! The squeezer machine. A clove of garlic goes in the little basket… SQUEEZE both handles… and out comes tiny garlic through the holes! Smelly, strong and delicious.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      This one is a name-it card: find the garlic press in the drawer, open and close the handles, maybe squeeze a clove with a grown-up’s hands on top. Smell the garlic after — the press’s whole party trick. Tools like this one are answered "that’s a garlic press — you’ll use one someday," which is exactly how future cooks are made.

      Quick parent note

      The Ages 6+ cards are "what is this?" cards: named, explored, understood — not yet used. The garlic press is a perfect one because its mechanism (a lever that squeezes) is visible and satisfying even for a watcher, and garlic is the smell kids recognize from across the house.

      Kettle Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Hot — don’t touch

      The gray kettle on the stovetop — the kettle boils the water for tea and cocoa, and it is the kitchen’s loudest safety teacher: kettle means HOT, and hot is a look-don’t-touch.

      Say it together

      “Kettle! The kettle boils the water. The kettle gets VERY hot — hot, hot, hot! We look at the kettle… we never touch the kettle. Only grown-ups use the kettle. Hands behind your back — safety pose!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Teach the safety pose: hands clasped behind the back, one big step back from the stove whenever the kettle is on. Say the rule the same way every time — "hot, don’t touch; grown-ups only" — and let your child be the safety checker who announces "the kettle is HOT!" when the steam starts. Rules said with a job attached are rules children keep.

      Quick parent note

      The kettle is the perfect first hot-things card because it announces itself: it whistles, it steams, it lives on the stove. A child who learns "the kettle is hot, I step back" has learned the pattern for every hot thing in the kitchen — the rule generalizes for free.

      Kitchen Timer Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The round dial with the numbers — the kitchen timer counts down the waiting, and the DING at the end is the best sound in baking: cookies are ready, the waiting is over.

      Say it together

      “Kitchen timer! Turn the dial to the number… tick, tick, tick… and — DING! The timer says when. Twelve minutes for the cookies — set the timer, and when it dings, the cookies are done!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hand the dial job over: your child sets the timer for cookies, for a ten-minute tidy-up, for "five more minutes of playground at home" (a carpet picnic). Watching the dial shrink makes time visible — and the DING is a celebration every single time. The timer turns waiting into a countdown game with a bell.

      Quick parent note

      The timer is the most quietly useful card in the set: it teaches that waiting has an end, that numbers count something real and that transitions come with a bell. Families who let the child own the dial report fewer "is it ready YET?" — the timer says it first.

      Teach it, step by step

      Ladle Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The long-handled deep spoon — the ladle scoops soup from the pot to the bowl, and serving the family their dinner is one of the proudest jobs a small cook can hold.

      Say it together

      “Ladle! The big deep spoon. Dip it in the soup… scoop… lift… pour into the bowl — there! One bowl of soup, served with care. Your turn to serve everyone!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Practise the scoop-pour with COLD soup or water in the sink first — dip, fill, carry, pour, no drips. Then promote it: ladling real (warm, not hot) soup into bowls at dinner, one bowl per person, counting them out. Serving the family is a big-kid job, and everyone says thank you.

      Quick parent note

      Ladling is a full command course: dip depth, fill control, steady carry, targeted pour. It also puts the child in the host’s seat — the one who feeds others. Few kitchen jobs earn as many genuine thank-yous, and thank-yous are fuel for more helping.

      Teach it, step by step

      Measuring Cup Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The clear jug with the lines on the side — the measuring cup counts the milk and the water for a recipe, and the lines on the side are numbers doing a job your child can see.

      Say it together

      “Measuring cup! The clear jug with the lines. Pour the milk in… stop at the line! The lines say how much. One cup of milk, exactly — that is measuring!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Set the jug on a level surface, crouch to eye level with the lines and pour slowly — milk creeping up to the line is surprisingly thrilling. Ask: "did we reach the line? A little more… STOP!" Then the measured milk goes into the real recipe. Numbers on a jug make the maths of baking visible and edible.

      Quick parent note

      Measuring is reading, maths and pouring control in one job — the clearest early-numbers practice outside a workbook, with a cake at the end. Eye-level reading of the line is a genuine science skill (parallax, taught later; understood now).

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      Measuring Spoons Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The little spoons on a ring — the measuring spoons count the small things: a spoon of sugar, a pinch of salt, a spoon of vanilla. Small scoops, big difference in the recipe.

      Say it together

      “Measuring spoons! The little scoops on a ring — big, medium, small, tiny. One spoon of sugar… level it flat with a finger… in it goes. Small spoons, exact amounts!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Let your child be the spoon-keeper: find the size the recipe asks for, scoop, level it flat by dragging a finger across the top, tip it in. Leveling is the secret skill — heaped spoons and level spoons bake differently. Five little scoops later, the cake knows the difference.

      Quick parent note

      Measuring spoons teach precision at the smallest scale — and leveling a spoon is fine-motor control at its neatest. The ring of sizes also invites ordering biggest-to-smallest, a free sorting game hiding on a kitchen counter.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      Microwave Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Hot — don’t touch

      The white box with the door and the buttons — the microwave heats food fast, and it comes with two hard rules kids learn early: grown-ups work the buttons, and the plate inside gets hot.

      Say it together

      “Microwave! The magic heating box. In goes the plate… beep beep… the food comes out WARM. The microwave is a grown-up machine — we watch, we wait for the beep, we never touch the plate. Hot, hot!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Teach the beep-and-wait ritual: food in (by a grown-up), buttons pressed (by a grown-up), then your child is the beep-watcher whose job is to announce "BEEP! It’s ready!" The job satisfies the curiosity, keeps small hands off the controls and makes the waiting part of the game. Steam comes out when the door opens — one more step back.

      Quick parent note

      The microwave’s two rules — grown-ups operate, plates get hot — are the same rules as the stove in smaller form. A child who waits for the beep has learned to wait for heat to cool, which is the habit that prevents most little-kitchen burns.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      Mixing Bowl Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Safe to use

      The big cream bowl with the green stripe — the mixing bowl is where the batter lives, and it is the natural throne of every little helper: everything worth stirring happens in here.

      Say it together

      “Mixing bowl! The big, big bowl. The flour goes in… the milk goes in… all in the mixing bowl. Now we stir! The bowl holds everything — no spills!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Set up the bowl on a damp cloth (it will not slide), and let your child be the pourer: cups of flour in, spoons of sugar in, cracks on the rim — the bowl catches everything. Naming it "the mixing bowl" gives the job an address, and jobs with addresses get done happily.

      Quick parent note

      A big bowl is safety equipment in disguise: wide walls catch spills, hold steady on the counter and give small arms room to stir big. The bowl also teaches the before-and-after of cooking — empty, then full — which is the first recipe a child ever reads.

      Teach it, step by step

      Mortar and Pestle Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 6+Grown-up tools

      The stone bowl and its grinding club — the mortar and pestle crushes herbs and seeds the way people have done for thousands of years. It might be the oldest kitchen tool on the whole shelf.

      Say it together

      “Mortar and pestle! The stone bowl and the grinding club. Seeds go in the bowl… grind, grind, grind in circles… the seeds become powder. People have used these since long, long ago!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name it, hold it, feel the weight — then watch a grown-up grind a few peppercorns or dried herbs and smell the difference: fresh-ground smells like the plant woke up. Try grinding a pinch of (safe, clean) rice with a grown-up’s hand guiding — heavy, slow, satisfying. Ancient tool, brand-new smell.

      Quick parent note

      The mortar and pestle is a history lesson hiding in a kitchen drawer — the same tool carved the same way fed the pharaohs. For the Ages 6+ crew the point is the question it answers: food did not always come pre-ground; someone crushed it, and now you know with what.

      Teach it, step by step

      Mug Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Safe to use

      The big cream cup with the handle — the mug is the grown-up cup, and being trusted with a real mug of warm cocoa is one of childhood’s great promotions.

      Say it together

      “Mug! The big cup with a handle. Two hands around the mug… careful… sip. Mugs are for warm drinks — cocoa, warm milk. Yum, just like the grown-ups!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Serve a child-size mug of warm (never hot) cocoa and teach the carry: two hands, walk slowly, set it down before you sip. The handle grip and the walking-with-liquid control are genuine skills — and being allowed a real mug tastes better than any drink.

      Quick parent note

      The mug card carries a built-in safety line: mugs are for WARM drinks, and grown-ups pour. The two-hand carry rule also transfers to every cup, jug and bowl the child will ever move — spill physics, learned early and gently.

      Teach it, step by step

      Oven Mitt Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The quilted green glove — the oven mitt is the glove that fights heat: slide it on and even a hot tray can be carried. It looks like a puppet and works like a shield.

      Say it together

      “Oven mitt! The thick, puffy glove. The mitt stops the heat — hot tray? No problem, the mitt says! Grown-ups wear the mitt for the hot things… and look — it fits your hand too, for the cool trays.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Wear the mitts for a puppet show first — mitts say hello, mitts give a high-five — so the glove is a friend before it is equipment. Then the real lesson: the mitt goes on BEFORE touching anything that was in the oven, and the grown-up’s hand goes under the child’s for anything properly hot. Mitt on, both hands, slow walk — the oven-to-counter parade.

      Quick parent note

      The oven mitt card teaches the WHY of kitchen safety gear: heat travels, the mitt blocks it. Children who understand the mitt’s job respect the hot things more, not less — because now they know exactly what heat does and exactly what stops it.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · KITCHEN THINGS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

      Peeler Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 6+Sharp — careful

      The green swivel tool with the hidden blade — the peeler takes the skin off carrots and potatoes in long ribbons, and its edge is sharp enough that it lives in the grown-up-tools family for now.

      Say it together

      “Peeler! The skin remover. It slides down the carrot… swish — long ribbons of skin fall off! The blade is sharp and hidden, so we LOOK with our eyes. Grown-ups peel; kids watch the ribbons fall.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name it, find it in the drawer, open and close the blade gently (grown-up fingers on the blade end). Then watch the peeling demo — the ribbons are the show — and collect them for the compost or a soup pot. The rule comes with it: the peeler’s edge is sharp even when it looks tiny, so it is a grown-up tool until hands grow bigger and steadier.

      Quick parent note

      The peeler looks harmless and is not — which is exactly why it is a great sharp-things teacher. Watching peels curl off in ribbons also answers a child question most adults never think to answer: where does the carrot’s skin GO? Into the ribbons, into the soup, into the compost — the whole loop, visible.

      Teach it, step by step

      Plate Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Safe to use

      The round cream plate with the green rim — the plate is where dinner lands, and the child who can set the table is not a guest at meals but part of the crew.

      Say it together

      “Plate! Here is your plate. One plate for you, one for me… set them on the table. The plate waits for the food. Yum!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make plate-setting the child’s job: one plate per seat, handed out with ceremony — "Daddy’s plate… Grandma’s plate… YOUR plate." Counting the seats and matching the plates is early maths at dinner speed. Then the empty plate to the sink finishes the job.

      Quick parent note

      A named plate gives a child ownership of their own eating space — picky eaters often accept food on "their" plate that they reject off it. And carrying a plate to the sink is the easiest first chore in the whole house.

      Refrigerator Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Safe to use

      The big gray two-door cupboard that hums — the refrigerator keeps the food cold so it stays good, and it is the most-visited appliance in the house, opening roughly forty times a day.

      Say it together

      “Refrigerator! The big, cold fridge. The milk lives in the fridge… the yogurt, the apples, the cheese. Brrr — the fridge keeps our food cold and fresh. Close the door so the cold stays in!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play fridge find-it: "bring me the milk… find the cheese… where do the eggs live?" Each trip teaches both the word and the food’s home. Then the door rule: one open, one close — the fridge works best when it is shut. A child who knows where food lives is a child who can help with every meal.

      Quick parent note

      The fridge is the kitchen’s landmark — every food conversation starts there. Naming it also teaches the why of cold: food goes bad when it is warm, the fridge keeps it cold, the food stays good. That little science story explains a hundred dinner-table mysteries.

      Teach it, step by step

      Rolling Pin Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The wooden roller with the green handles — the rolling pin flattens the dough for cookies and pies, and rolling it back and forth is one of the great satisfying jobs of baking.

      Say it together

      “Rolling pin! Hold both handles… push — roll, roll, roll! The dough gets flat and thin. Roll it this way, roll it that way… even all over. Ready for the cookie cutters!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Flour the counter, divide the dough and let your child roll their own piece flat — two hands, long pushes, edge to edge. Then cut cookies and compare shapes. A flat, even sheet is a real skill with a real score: the cookies themselves. Uneven cookies taste exactly the same, which keeps the joy safe.

      Quick parent note

      Rolling is two-hand coordination, pressure control and patience — the whole upper body works. It is also the baking job with the lowest stakes and the highest sensory payoff: cool dough, dusty flour, the slow squash of the pin. Bakers are made at the rolling-pin stage.

      Teach it, step by step

      Saucepan Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Hot — don’t touch

      The silver pot with the long handle — the saucepan makes the soup, the pasta and the porridge, and it lives on the stove, which makes it a member of the hot, don’t-touch family.

      Say it together

      “Saucepan! The pot that cooks the soup. The saucepan sits on the stove and gets VERY hot — hot, hot, hot! We never touch the saucepan. Grown-ups stir the pot; we stir our pretend pot over here.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Give the saucepan rule its own voice every time it is on the stove — "the pot is hot, step back" — then offer the safe twin: a toy pot at the play table where your child cooks the same meal with a wooden spoon. The pretend pot takes the real pot’s temptation away, and the rule does the rest.

      Quick parent note

      Hot pan + short person + reaching hand is the classic kitchen accident, which is why this card exists: the pot is named, the rule is rehearsed and the safe alternative is always offered. Turn pot handles inward on the stove — the reaching game ends before it starts.

      Teach it, step by step

      Spatula Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The flat green turning tool — the spatula slides under pancakes and cookies and flips them over, and it is the tool every kid wants to hold on pancake morning.

      Say it together

      “Spatula! The flat flipper. Slide it under the pancake… lift… and FLIP! Over it goes. The spatula turns food over so both sides cook. Sizzle… flip… sizzle!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Practise the flip on a COLD pan with a piece of bread or a foam pancake — slide, lift, turn, no panic. Then hand the spatula over for the real flip (grown-up’s hand hovering, pan off the heat for the moment). One successful pancake flip is a breakfast legend that gets retold for years.

      Quick parent note

      The flip is precision work: slide depth, lift speed, wrist turn. Practising on a cold pan removes every burn risk while keeping all the skill. And the spatula job pairs perfectly with the frying-pan card’s rule — the pan stays hot and untouched; the spatula does the reaching.

      Strainer Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 6+Grown-up tools

      The fine mesh net on a handle — the strainer is the colander’s careful cousin: its holes are so small they catch flour dust and tea leaves, letting only the liquid slip through.

      Say it together

      “Strainer! The net with the handle. The mesh is tiny — it catches the flour lumps, the seeds, the bits… and lets the liquid run through clean. Sift, strain, drip drip. The strainer is the careful one!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name it next to the colander — same idea, finer net — and test the pair: which catches flour? Which catches pasta? Then watch a grown-up dust a cake with icing sugar through the strainer: a snowfall of sugar, all from the mesh. The strainer’s magic is its smallness — holes too small to see, big enough to matter.

      Quick parent note

      Strainer and colander make a beautiful compare-and-contrast pair for the Ages 6+ shelf: same job, different hole size, different catches. Understanding "the mesh chooses what passes" is early engineering thinking — and icing-sugar snowfalls are unbeatable theater.

      Toaster Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Hot — don’t touch

      The gray box with the two slots — the toaster turns bread into toast, and it comes with the kitchen’s most specific rule: the slots are for bread, never for fingers, never for forks.

      Say it together

      “Toaster! Bread goes in the slots… press the lever down — CLUNK! It gets warm and… POP! Toast jumps up! Only bread goes in the toaster — never fingers, never forks. Grown-ups help with the toast.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Let your child drop the bread in (with a grown-up beside them) and be the lever-presser — CLUNK is a deeply satisfying sound. When the POP comes, the grown-up lifts the toast out. The rule is said every time, same words: bread in, toast out, no fingers, no forks.

      Quick parent note

      The toaster teaches two lessons at once: a routine (bread, lever, wait, pop) and the first "never put metal in it" rule that will generalize to every appliance. Toast is also the breakfast a three-year-old can help make from start to butter — pride served warm.

      Tongs Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The two green arms that grab — the tongs pick up food and small things without fingers ever touching them, and squeezing them open and shut is a game all by itself.

      Say it together

      “Tongs! The grabber arms. Squeeze to open… let go to grab! Pick up the pom-pom… squeeze… carry… drop in the bowl. Tongs are fingers that live on a stick!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Set up the tong relay: pom-poms or cotton balls moved from one bowl to another, one squeeze at a time. Then the real job — serving salad at dinner or picking up marshmallows for cocoa, tongs-only, no fingers allowed. The squeeze-and-carry grip is the exact muscle pattern pencils ask for later.

      Quick parent note

      Tongs are a fine-motor classic: the open-squeeze rhythm builds hand strength and control better than most toys, disguised as a job. They also teach a lovely idea — tools can be extra fingers — which is the whole secret of kitchens and workshops alike.

      Trash Bin Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Safe to use

      The gray bin with the green lid — the trash bin is where the wrappers and peels go, and it has the best doorbell in the kitchen: step on the pedal, the lid opens, in it goes.

      Say it together

      “Trash bin! The wrapper goes in the bin. Step on the pedal… the lid opens… in it goes — whoosh! All tidy. The bin keeps our kitchen clean.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make your child the bin chief for a day: every wrapper, every peel, every scrap goes in by THEIR pedal-and-toss. Then hand them the kitchen’s easiest real chore — emptying the little scraps bowl after dinner. Pedal, toss, close. Two-year-olds can do it; five-year-olds do it without being asked.

      Quick parent note

      A named bin gives mess a destination, which halves the "where does this go?" questions. The pedal is also perfect for toddlers — it works by foot, so hands stay clean and the lid-opening feels like magic. Small bin jobs grow into real tidy habits.

      Whisk Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Safe to use

      The balloon-shaped beater — the whisk turns eggs fluffy and cream into clouds, and it is the helper tool that feels the most like magic: fast circles in, foam out.

      Say it together

      “Whisk! The bouncy wire whisk. Hold the handle… whisk whisk whisk — fast circles! Look, the eggs have bubbles! The whisk makes fluffy eggs and fluffy cream.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Crack three eggs into the mixing bowl, hand over the whisk and time the whipping — can you make bubbles in thirty seconds? Wrist circles are hard work and enormously satisfying. The whisked eggs go straight into scrambled eggs, and the cook who whisked them eats prouder every time.

      Quick parent note

      Whisking is genuine wrist and forearm exercise — the same motion writing will later ask for. It also shows cause and effect at top speed: effort in, foam out, instantly. A four-year-old who whisks the eggs never has to be asked to try them.
